content: Infants diagnosed with HIV within the first year of life should begin antiretroviral therapy (ART) immediately, regardless of their clinical stage or CD4 cell count. This is a strong recommendation based on moderate-quality evidence. For children aged 1 to less than 10 years, ART initiation is also recommended, though this is a conditional recommendation supported by low-quality evidence. Priority should be given to children under 2 years of age or those younger than 5 years with advanced HIV disease (WHO clinical stage 3 or 4) or low CD4 counts (≤750 cells/mm³ or CD4 percentage <25%). For children aged 5 years and older, ART should be initiated if they have advanced HIV disease or CD4 counts ≤350 cells/mm³. These recommendations are strongly supported by moderate-quality evidence. Adolescents aged 10–19 years living with HIV should start ART regardless of their clinical stage or CD4 count. Priority should be given to those with severe or advanced HIV disease (WHO stage 3 or 4) or CD4 counts ≤350 cells/mm³. These recommendations are conditional and based on low-quality evidence. For HIV-positive individuals with tuberculosis (TB), ART should be initiated in all cases, regardless of CD4 count. TB treatment should begin first, followed by ART within the first 8 weeks of TB treatment. For patients with very low CD4 counts (<50 cells/mm³), ART should be started within the first 2 weeks of TB treatment. These are strong recommendations supported by high-quality evidence. For adolescents starting first-line ART, the preferred regimen includes two nucleoside reverse transcriptase inhibitors (NRTIs) plus either a non-nucleoside reverse transcriptase inhibitor (NNRTI) or an integrase strand transfer inhibitor (INSTI). The recommended combination is tenofovir (TDF) + lamivudine (3TC) or emtricitabine (FTC) + efavirenz (EFV) as a fixed-dose combination. Alternative regimens include TDF + 3TC (or FTC) + dolutegravir (DTG) or EFV 400 mg. If these regimens are contraindicated or unavailable, other options such as abacavir (ABC) + 3TC + EFV or zidovudine (AZT) + 3TC + EFV may be used. These recommendations are strong but based on lowto moderate-quality evidence. For children aged 3 to less than 10 years, the NRTI backbone for ART should preferably include ABC + 3TC or AZT/TDF + 3TC (or FTC). For children younger than 3 years, the NRTI backbone should include ABC or AZT + 3TC. Where viral load monitoring is available, lopinavir/ritonavir (LPV/r) may be substituted with EFV at 3 years of age if viral suppression is sustained. These are strong recommendations supported by moderate-quality evidence. Routine viral load monitoring is recommended at 6 months, 12 months, and annually thereafter for patients stable on ART. In settings with routine viral load monitoring, CD4 cell count monitoring can be discontinued for individuals who are stable and virally suppressed. Dried blood spot specimens can be used to determine HIV viral load, with a threshold of 1,000 copies/mL to define virological failure. These are conditional recommendations based on lowto very low-quality evidence. For second-line ART in children, those younger than 3 years failing a first-line LPV/r-based regimen should switch to a raltegravir (RAL)-based second-line regimen. Children older than 3 years should switch to a second-line regimen containing two NRTIs plus EFV or RAL. For those failing a first-line NNRTI-based regimen, a boosted protease inhibitor (PI)-based regimen, such as LPV/r or atazanavir/ritonavir (ATV/r), is preferred. These are conditional recommendations supported by very low-quality evidence. For adults and adolescents requiring second-line ART, a heat-stable fixed-dose combination of darunavir/ritonavir (DRV/r) can be used as an alternative boosted PI option. A combination of RAL plus LPV/r is also an alternative. National programs should develop policies for third-line ART, which should include new drugs with minimal cross-resistance, such as INSTIs and second-generation NNRTIs and PIs. Patients failing second-line regimens with no new ARV options should continue a tolerated regimen. These are conditional recommendations based on low-quality evidence. For Kaposi sarcoma in HIV-infected individuals, immediate ART initiation is recommended for mild/moderate disease. For severe/symptomatic disease, ART should be combined with systemic chemotherapy, such as vincristine, bleomycin, and doxorubicin (ABV), or liposomal anthracyclines when available. These are strong recommendations supported by low-quality evidence. For seborrheic dermatitis, mild cases should be treated with topical ketoconazole 2% two to three times per week for four weeks, with maintenance treatment as needed. Severe cases should prompt HIV testing, and ART initiation should be assessed if positive. For papular pruritic eruption and eosinophilic folliculitis, ART is the primary treatment. For molluscum contagiosum, ART is recommended for extensive or unusual cases, with no additional specific treatment required. For oropharyngeal candidiasis in children, oral fluconazole is the preferred treatment. Topical therapies such as nystatin suspension or clotrimazole troches are alternatives. Prompt ART initiation is recommended for all HIV-infected individuals with oropharyngeal candidiasis. For Stevens-Johnson syndrome or toxic epidermal necrolysis in HIV-infected individuals, the suspected causative drug should be discontinued immediately, and supportive therapies provided. Systemic corticosteroids are not recommended. Nutritional care for HIV-infected children should include initial nutritional assessment and regular growth monitoring at each visit, integrated with ART response evaluation. Children should be managed according to a nutrition care plan to meet their specific needs. For acute seizures in children without IV access, non-parenteral benzodiazepines such as rectal diazepam or intranasal/oral midazolam should be used. If IV access is available, IV diazepam or lorazepam is preferred. For persistent seizures, IV valproate, phenobarbital, or phenytoin may be used, with valproate preferred due to its superior benefit-risk profile. Antiepileptic drugs should not be routinely prescribed after a first unprovoked seizure. For febrile seizures, prophylactic treatment with antipyretics or anticonvulsants is not recommended. Diagnostic tests such as blood glucose and lumbar puncture should be performed in children with acute seizures or altered consciousness, particularly in febrile children with signs of meningitis. Pulse oximetry is recommended to detect hypoxemia and guide oxygen therapy in children with severe respiratory infections. Oxygen therapy should be provided to children with oxygen saturation ≤90% at altitudes ≤2,500 m or ≤87% at higher altitudes. Nasal prongs are the preferred method for oxygen delivery in children under 5 years. Oxygen therapy can be discontinued when oxygen saturation remains stable above the recommended levels for at least 15 minutes on room air.
